OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
For any $k\geq 2$ let $g_k(n)$ denote the maximum value of\[(a_1+\cdots+a_k)-n\]where $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ are integers such that $a_1!\cdots a_k! \mid n!$. Can one show that\[\sum_{n\leq x}g_k(n) \sim c_k x\log x\]for some constant $c_k$? Is it true that there is a constant $c_k$ such that for almost all $n<x$ we have\[g_k(n)=c_k\log x+o(\log x)?\]
#400: [ErGr80,p.77]
number theory | 
factorials
Erdős and Graham write that it is easy to show that $g_k(n) \ll_k \log n$ always, but the best possible constant is unknown.
See also [401].

 Numerical data for $g_2(n)$ up to $n=10^5$
I have computed exact values of $g_2(n)$ for all $2 \le n \le 10^5$ and posted the code and data at github.com/peter-rich/erdos-problem-400-numerics.
By Legendre's formula, $a!\,b! \mid n!$ iff\[
a+b-n \;\le\; s_p(a)+s_p(b)-s_p(n)
\quad\text{for every prime }p,
\]where $s_p$ is the base-$p$ digit sum. The script searches the excess $E=a+b-n$ downward from an upper bound; candidates are filtered by the digit-sum inequality at small primes (vectorised), and survivors are verified against all primes $p \le n$ by exact valuations. Every reported value is exact.
Dyadic-window means of $g_2(n)/\log n$ increase monotonically: $1.126$ on $[2^{12},2^{13}]$ up to $\approx 1.262$ on $[2^{16},10^5]$. They pass strictly above the lower-bound coefficient $3/\log 12 \approx 1.2073$ with no sign of levelling off.
The summatory ratio
$\frac{1}{x\log x}\sum_{n\le x} g_2(n) \;\approx\; 1.103
\quad\text{at }x=10^5;
$
first-order extrapolation gives $\approx 1.21$ and rising.
The data suggests that if the constant $c_2$ exists then $c_2 > 1.25$, strictly above the current density-one lower bound of Li (arXiv:2606.23661) and well below the pointwise upper bound $1/\log 2 \approx 1.4427$.
At maximizers the $p=2$ constraint binds with $p=3$ secondary: optimal pairs $(a,b)$ are simultaneously digit-dense in bases $2$ and $3$, and $g_2(n)$ is small when $s_2(n)+s_3(n)$ is large (e.g.\ $g_2(2^6-1)=8$).
Runtime: $\approx 4.5$ minutes for $N=10^5$ (single core, NumPy + SymPy).
None of this resolves \#400, but it is numerical evidence intended to indicate which side of the bracket is loose.

 Using a recent result of Pomerance, one gets the lower bound\[
\sum_{n\le x} g_k(n) \gg_k x\log x
\]for every fixed \(k\ge 2\).
Indeed, by Theorem 1 here: https://math.colgate.edu/~integers/aa47/aa47.pdf, for every fixed \(\eta<1/\log 4\), there is a set \(S_\eta\) of asymptotic density \(1\) such that, for every \(m\in S_\eta\) and every positive integer \(r\le \eta\log m\),\[
\frac{(m+r)!}{m!}\mid {2m\choose m}.
\]Taking \(r=\lfloor \eta\log m\rfloor\), this gives\[
m!(m+r)! \mid (2m)!.
\]Hence, in the definition of \(g_k(2m)\), we may take\[
a_1=m+r,\qquad a_2=m,\qquad a_3=\cdots=a_k=1,
\]and obtain\[
g_k(2m)\ge r+k-2\ge \lfloor\eta\log m\rfloor .
\]Therefore, with \(M=\lfloor x/2\rfloor\),\[
\sum_{n\le x}g_k(n)
\ge
\sum_{\substack{m\le M\\ m\in S_\eta}}\lfloor\eta\log m\rfloor
=
\left(\frac{\eta}{2}+o(1)\right)x\log x.
\]Since this holds for every \(\eta<1/\log4\),\[
\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{1}{x\log x}\sum_{n\le x}g_k(n)
\ge \frac{1}{2\log4}.
\]Together with the standard upper bound \(g_k(n)\ll_k\log n\), this gives the correct order of magnitude for the summatory function, although not the asymptotic constant.
With some optimization, I think I can get $c_k \ge \frac{k - 1}{\log{4}}$, but the correct constant is likely $\frac{k - 1}{\log{2}}$ as mentioned in the upper bound comment.

 This seems problematic - as Eric Li notes this paper was heavily created/written by ChatGPT, which tends to first of all look at the remarks and comments on this site when asked to prove something. Presumably it used the remarks here as a starting point. It therefore seems disingenuous to not mention your remarks. 
But this is part of a wider question about how we should be assigning 'credit' for a solution in this new age of AI.
(Also as a side note this paper is clearly heavily, if not entirely, AI-written and so, as usual, it is difficult to read and likely misses important citations and context, and presumably a human-written version would be shorter, perhaps more powerful, and certainly be more pleasant to read.)

 FWIW, here's what Erdős and Graham probably had in mind: The condition is equivalent to $\sum_i \nu_p(a_i!)\le \nu_p(n!)$ for all $p$. This is equivalent to $\sum_i a_i-s_p(a_i)\le n-s_p(n)$, or $(a_1+\dots+a_k)-n\le s_p(a_1)+\dots+s_p(a_k)-s_p(n)$. If you take $p=2$ for example, you get that $g_k(n)\le \log_2(a_1)+\dots+\log_2(a_k)+O_k(1)\le k\log n+O_k(1)$. This yields the $g_k(n)\ll_k \log n$.
This idea in fact gives the upper bound $c_k\le \frac{k-1/2}{\log 2}$. Getting a lower bound seems difficult in comparison. Really, the bottleneck should be $p=2$.
